author: yellaber
body:
## Por qué

El contrato describía qué puede hacer un `administrador`, pero no de dónde sale el primero.

`POST /usuarios/registro` asigna `validador` sin excepción y `PATCH /usuarios/{id}/rol` exige ya ser administrador. Sobre una base de datos vacía el rol era **inalcanzable por API**, y con él las cuatro operaciones de administración de cuentas (listar, consultar, cambiar rol, cambiar estado). El único escape era un `UPDATE` manual sobre Postgres — fuera del contrato, fuera de la API y fuera de toda traza.

Es lo último que separa al MVP publicado (v0.1.0) de un sistema que se puede poner en marcha sin tocar la base de datos a mano.

## Qué cambia en el contrato

- **`POST /sistema/inicializar`** — crea la cuenta administradora de origen y marca el sistema como inicializado. Responde `201` con el `Usuario` creado (`rol: administrador`, `estado: activo`), **sin sesión**: el administrador entra después por `POST /usuarios/login`.
- **De un solo uso.** Toda llamada posterior responde `409 CONFLICTO` **aunque el secreto sea correcto**: el secreto autoriza la operación, no la vuelve repetible. No existe operación de reversa.
- **`securityScheme` `bootstrapToken`** (`apiKey` en la cabecera `X-Bootstrap-Token`), fijado por el operador en el entorno del despliegue. La operación declara `security: [bootstrapToken]`, no `security: []`.
- **`tag` `sistema`** — el primero que no corresponde a un módulo de dominio; acotado en su descripción al ciclo de vida de la instalación.
- **`InicializarSistemaRequest`** con las mismas reglas de validación que `RegistroUsuarioRequest`.

`POST /usuarios/registro` **queda intacto**: sigue siendo público y sigue asignando `validador`, antes y después de la inicialización. Ningún endpoint existente se modifica y no se añade ningún código de error — `NO_AUTENTICADO`, `CONFLICTO` y `VALIDACION_FALLIDA` ya estaban en el catálogo.

## La decisión de fondo

Un endpoint de inicialización sin protección sería funcional, pero abre una **ventana de reclamación**: entre el instante en que la API queda expuesta y el instante en que el operador la llama, cualquiera que llegue primero se queda con el administrador del sistema — y el candado de un solo uso hace esa pérdida irreversible. Es una familia de vulnerabilidad con historial en productos reales (el asistente de instalación que quedó abierto).

El secreto de despliegue cierra esa ventana sin renunciar a nada: sigue siendo una llamada HTTP, sin necesidad de acceso por consola.

El razonamiento completo, con las alternativas descartadas (rol especial en el registro, ventana temporal en vez de secreto, promover en vez de crear), está en `design.md`.

## Verificación

- `openspec validate --strict` — válido.
- `redocly lint` — **20 errores y 3 avisos, idéntico a `develop`**; ninguno cae en lo añadido. Los 20 son todos el mismo problema preexistente: `nullable` en un documento `openapi: 3.1.0`, donde esa propiedad ya no existe. Ajeno a este PR, pero es deuda real del contrato y daría para un change propio.
- Diff revisado: solo `contrato-api/openapi.yaml`, las dos enumeraciones de `tags` en `CLAUDE.md` / `README.md`, y los artefactos del change. **Sin código de runtime.**

## Riesgo conocido, documentado en `design.md`

No hay recuperación si se pierde el acceso a la única cuenta administradora: la inicialización ya se consumió y no existe reversa. La mitigación dentro del contrato es promover a un segundo administrador con `PATCH /usuarios/{id}/rol` nada más entrar, así que lo prudente es dejar **dos** desde el principio.

## Después de este PR

1. `docs/archivar-contrato-api-inicializacion-del-sistema` — archiva el change y promueve `sistema` a capacidad.
2. Change de backend `inicializacion-del-sistema` — implementa el endpoint: módulo `sistema`, marcador de inicialización persistido (que resuelve además la carrera entre llamadas simultáneas) y el secreto validado al arranque con el resto de la configuración.

author: jafin
body:
Implements spec 23 — *One implementation per style interface: delete the deferred facades* — tasks 1 through 5.

`IXLStyle.Batch` was a **second parallel implementation** of seven style interfaces rather than a flush policy on the one facade. Which implementation a caller got was decided inside `XLStyle.Batch`, so `cell.Style.Border.X = v` and `cell.Style.Batch(s => s.Border.X = v)` ran different code for the same assignment, on the same container, through the same interface.

This makes batching a mode on `XLStyle` and deletes the twin — **713 lines**, seven files.

## The defect this closes

`XLBorder.InsideBorder` is container-aware: a cell's `RangesUsed` is a 1×1 range, which has no interior edges, so `RestoreOutsideBorder` captures and restores all four edges and the net effect is correctly nothing. `XLDeferredBorder.InsideBorder` had no container and could not know that — it was byte-identical to its own `OutsideBorder` setter three lines above.

```csharp
cell.Style.Border.InsideBorder = XLBorderStyleValues.Thick;               // no-op    (correct)
cell.Style.Batch(s => s.Border.InsideBorder = XLBorderStyleValues.Thick); // all four (wrong)
```

Fixed by deletion, not by a patch: the batch path now runs the same `XLBorder`.

## Commits

| Task | Commit |
|---|---|
| 1 | `test(style)`: parity test for every border property — **committed red** |
| 2 | `refactor(style)`: `XLStyle` gains the pending-key batching mode (inert) |
| 3 | `refactor(style)`: facades read their key from the style while it batches |
| 4 | `refactor(style)`: route `Batch` through the mode; delete the seven deferred types |
| 5 | `perf(style)`: pending key as loose components in a pooled holder |
| 5 | `perf(style)`: read the component key once per setter, off the pending holder directly |
| — | `fix(style)`: refresh the cached component facades when a batch flushes |

## Task 1 found less than the spec predicted

**13 of 14 argument sets passed, not 12.** Only `InsideBorder` failed. `XLDeferredBorder.InsideBorderColor` does write all four edge colours, but every edge is styleless and `XLBorderKey.Normalize` resets a styleless edge's colour to black when the key is resolved — so the bug was real but invisible in the resulting key. The parity set is narrower than analysed, not wider, so tasks 2–4 were unaffected.

## Task 5 caught two regressions and fixed both at cause

**Pass 1.** The pending key as an `XLStyleKey?` field on `XLStyle` cost **more** than the object graph it replaced, in two separable ways the new benchmark isolates:

* `XLStyleKey` is a large struct and an `XLStyle` is allocated per cell on the ordinary styling path, so holding one inline grew every style. `DirectPerCell` — code this PR does not otherwise touch — went from 32.5 ms / 29.1 MB to **42.0 ms / 42.1 MB**.
* Every `with` on that key copies the whole struct and re-runs the assigned component's `init` accessor, which normalizes and re-hashes it. A six-property batch paid six copies and six component hashes that it then paid again at flush. `BatchPerCell` went from 29.5 ms to **72.0 ms**.

`XLStyle.PendingKey` now holds loose component fields behind one reference, assembles the `XLStyleKey` exactly once at flush, and is rented from a one-deep per-thread cache instead of allocated per batch.

**Pass 2.** That still left batching at a 0.93 `Batch`/`Direct` ratio against a pre-spec 0.90. The deferred twins exposed their component key as a bare field and their setters just wrote it — no equality guard, no container test, one read — whereas the real facades read `Key` twice per assignment (guard, then the `with`), and each read had come to cost two null tests. So: `XLStyle` exposes the pending holder directly, making a facade's `Key` getter one field read and one null test; and every setter reads `Key` once into a local and reuses it. Both behaviour-preserving.

### Numbers

**Read the ratio, not the milliseconds.** This machine drifts hard between sessions: `ValueOnly` in `CellStylingBenchmarks` — which touches no style code at all — moved 8.9% across two sweeps of identical binaries, and pre-spec `BatchPerCell` measured 29.5 ms in one session and 32.3 ms in another. A cross-session millisecond delta under ~10% is not evidence of anything here. The within-run ratio cancels that drift; the allocation columns are exact.

`BatchStylingBenchmarks`, 50,000 cells × 6 properties, net10.0, medians of three runs, all three variants measured back to back in one thermal window:

| Variant | `BatchPerCell` | `Batch`/`Direct` | Batch allocation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pre-spec (`1b41cadd`) | 32.33 ms | 0.90 | 32.16 MB |
| Branch, before pass 2 | 32.20 ms | 0.93 | 29.49 MB |
| **Branch, final** | **31.41 ms** | **0.90** | **29.49 MB** |

Batch is back to its pre-spec ratio against direct assignment, allocates 8.3% less than the deferred graph did, and no longer provokes gen1 collections on the batch path.

`DirectPerCell` allocation is 29.48 MB against a pre-spec 29.10 MB — a deterministic **+8 bytes per `XLStyle`**, the one `_pending` reference field. Every `CellStylingBenchmarks` variant that builds a per-cell facade gained exactly +0.77 MB over 100,000 cells and the three that do not are byte-identical, which is what makes that attribution certain rather than inferred. Normalised to `ValueOnly` within each session, every per-cell styling ratio is flat or better than pre-spec.

## Also fixed: a retained facade went stale across a batch

**Pre-existing, not fallout from this PR** — both cases below fail identically at the merge-base. Fixed here because the flush is now the one place that can see it.

A component facade the caller obtained before or during a `Batch` stays reachable afterwards, and outside a batch a facade reads its key from its own cached value. That value was never updated at flush, so a retained facade reported pre-batch values — and a later write through it rebuilt the component key from them, silently dropping everything the batch had set:

```csharp
var font = cell.Style.Font;
cell.Style.Batch(s => s.Font.FontSize = 20);
font.Italic = true;                 // FontSize reverts to 11
```

`XLStyle`'s own component getters resync on every access, which is why only a facade the caller *keeps hold of* is affected, and why no existing test caught it.

The border is **refreshed rather than synced**. `XLBorder.SyncValue` drops the pending edge colours when the incoming key differs — right when the style moved underneath the facade, wrong at a flush, where the facade's own writes are what moved it. Blanket-syncing would have broken this, which the direct path gets right:

```csharp
cell.Style.Batch(s => { s.Border.LeftBorder = Thin; s.Border.TopBorderColor = Red; });
cell.Style.Border.TopBorder = Thin;   // must paint the top edge red
```

The colour is held pending because the top edge is styleless, and the direct path keeps it across exactly this transition via `SetKey`. So `XLBorder` gains a `RefreshValue` that assigns the value and leaves the pendings alone. `A_colour_left_pending_by_a_batch_still_applies_afterwards` pins it against the direct-path equivalent, and was checked to fail when the border is synced instead of refreshed — a gate that can actually fail, not one that merely passes.

Benchmarks unmoved: `Batch`/`Direct` ratio 0.91 median of three, batch allocation 29.49 MB.

## Two deviations from the spec text

Both forced by the code, both documented at their site.

1. **`XLStyle.Key` reads through the pending key**, rather than a separate `CurrentKey` leaving `Key` on `Value.Key`. `RestoreOutsideBorder` reads a cell's key back through `XLStyle.Key` mid-edit, so a compound inside-border operation inside a batch would otherwise capture the pre-batch key and restore over assignments the same batch had already made.
2. **Facades read through the style only while it is batching**, keeping `_value` as the source of truth otherwise, rather than dropping `_value` entirely. `XLFont(IXLFontBase)`, `XL

author: steipete
body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users with a direct-loopback Chrome extension pairing lose browser automation when no local Gateway or browser node is serving the relay. A tunnel to a remote Gateway does not supply that same-host relay.

The originally reviewed implementation also woke the first configured extension profile instead of the port in the reconnecting extension's pairing. A later or explicitly pinned profile could receive `spawned` while its actual relay remained absent.

## Why This Change Was Made

The browser plugin owns a standalone relay daemon, started on demand by the exact-origin-validated native messaging host. Port binding retains single-instance ownership; existing listeners are left alone. The daemon uses the existing host-local key, defaults to mutual v2 authentication, honors only an explicit legacy-auth opt-in, and exits after the idle grace when neither the extension nor a CDP client remains connected.

The extension now carries its canonical direct-loopback `relayPort` in `ensure_relay`. After caller and manifest validation, the host checks that port against current resolved extension profiles before probing or spawning. Missing, malformed, duplicate, extra, unconfigured, removed-profile, and managed-browser targets fail closed. Bootstrap retains its existing three-field request and Gateway route. No remote secret copying, direct DevTools fallback, Gateway service, protocol-version bump, or database migration is added.

The relay-key reader also enforces POSIX owner/mode checks. The existing bounded exclusive-writer handoff is preserved, including the briefly empty-file case inside that handoff. Unused production exports and unnecessary assertions were removed instead of weakening CI guards; the assertion baseline shrank.

## User Impact

On macOS and Linux, an updated extension and native host can recover a configured direct-loopback pairing without a running local Gateway. Non-first and explicitly pinned extension profiles wake their own relay. Automatic-setup opt-out, pairing revocation, and remote/Gateway-route boundaries remain respected.

This does not change automatic local bootstrap into a standalone pairing. Gateway-route pairings remain Gateway-route pairings. Store-build wake-up availability is not claimed; source-build validation requires the updated bundled unpacked extension. Windows retains manual setup.

## Evidence

Current candidate: `6637eb2aaaafbf63291885fa60618a6e8574aa58`, refreshed without conflicts onto main snapshot `8dac217ce94e14a67ad2fc65837e518a2fbe0669`.

The refresh was necessary because the old candidate supported state schema 9 and refused an installed schema-12 state database. The refreshed source supports schema 12. No operator database was downgraded or migrated.

- Before the targeting repair, the added non-first and pinned native-frame regressions failed with `invalid_request`. Both now pass through the real framing/configuration/relay boundary.
- Before the writer-handoff repair, the regression reproduced the safe reader throwing on the briefly empty exclusive-created key file. It passes with the bounded reread restored.
- Refreshed focused suite: **11 files passed, 299 tests passed, one skipped**.
- Full `pnpm build`: passed, with the built artifact recording the candidate SHA.
- Whole-PR `check-changed`: all selected checks passed, including core/UI/plugin/script/test types, lint, boundaries, ratchets, dead exports, and runtime import cycles. No required gate was skipped.
- Targeted formatting and `git diff --check`: passed.
- Fresh full-PR Codex autoreview: no actionable findings at its configured P0 threshold. This does not clear the runtime-proof blockers below.
- One complete original-order real-process run passed using the built CLI, native host, and daemon with isolated synthetic state. It verified non-first automatic and pinned targets, untouched first-profile ports, rejected unconfigured/removed targets, unchanged bootstrap, rejected caller origin, mutual v2 authentication, default legacy refusal, repeated `running` status, and cleanup.

The first refreshed build exposed a stale dependency install; a frozen-lockfile install resolved it without package or lockfile edits. One Gateway-route integration test timed out during the initial concurrent build. The final focused rerun passed without that build/check contention; no timeout or assertion was weakened.

### Remaining landing blockers

**This is not an all-green or land-ready report.**

1. **Cold CLI startup remains intermittent.** The unchanged CLI-first process probe passed once, with metadata by 19.607 seconds, then timed out in fresh state at the unchanged 30-second bound with zero output. A profiled diagnostic reproduced the timeout. Repeated plugin metadata discovery and browser registration dominate the captured filesystem work, but a safe metadata-lifetime repair has not been established. Those CLI/metadata sources are unchanged by this PR. No larger timeout, native-first warm-up, global cache bypass, or browser-specific shortcut is presented as a fix. A read-only candidate installation-status command against the existing host state also timed out at 30 seconds with zero output.
2. **Current-candidate, source-blind existing-profile Chrome proof is incomplete.** Native GUI setup returned refused or indeterminate verified-input results, so input attempts were stopped and re-observed instead of guessed or replayed blindly. No Chrome restart, operator Gateway mutation, direct DevTools fallback, or isolated-browser substitute was used. Earlier live proof is not evidence for this refreshed candidate.

Exact-head hosted [CI run 33041072708](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/33041072708) passed on candidate `6637eb2aaaafbf63291885fa60618a6e8574aa58` on its first attempt. Native prepare/merge will not run while the two runtime-proof blockers above remain.

### Reproduction commands

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/browser/src/browser/extension-native-host.test.ts extensions/browser/chrome-extension/modules/native-bootstrap.test.ts extensions/browser/chrome-extension/modules/relay-core.test.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/extension-relay-daemon-spawn.test.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/relay-daemon.test.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/extension-relay/relay-auth.test.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/config.test.ts extensions/browser/chrome-extension/background.test.ts extensions/browser/chrome-extension/background.access-mode.test.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/extension-pairing.test.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/extension-relay/gateway-relay-route.integration.test.ts
```

```bash
node scripts/check-changed.mjs --base 8dac217ce94e14a67ad2fc65837e518a2fbe0669 --head 6637eb2aaaafbf63291885fa60618a6e8574aa58 --timed
```

```bash
pnpm build
```

### Review follow-through and scope

Both previously listed rank-up moves are implemented: carry and validate the stored pairing target, and cover non-first/pinned profiles. The serialized-state notice referred to test fixtures; this PR adds no persistent schema.

Production LOC: **+433/-42, net +391**. Tests: **+584/-1, net +583**. Docs: +62/-14. Tooling: +2/-1. Production growth supplies the daemon lifecycle, targeted native request, configuration validation, and key-read protection. The refresh itself added no source or test changes.

Named follow-up: prepare plugin metadata once within the correct CLI lifetime across output detection, owner lookup, and registration, while preserving scoped-discovery and configuration-policy boundaries. A separate pre-existing initial-read key-creation race also remains outside the repaired EEXIST reread path; it should be reproduced and fixed at the same credential owner without weakening validation.

author: zhuyue11
body:
**Repository 2 of 2 for MOTIR-3264** — the paired change is [motir-gateway#20](https://github.com/moooon-B-V/motir-gateway/pull/20) (`fly.toml` comments). Same branch name in both and both titles carry the key: the card carries a repository SET, so it stays In Review until **both** have merged.

This half is criterion 4 — §21's `motir-gateway` row, its *"does a second warm machine add compute-hours?"* cell, and the paragraph MOTIR-3257 added naming this defect as unowned (`**It has no owner yet.**`, now replaced by the outcome). **The 2026-08-13 and 2026-08-20 measurement tables are left exactly as written** — they are true records of what was measured then, and the second one is the evidence for this card's main finding.

## Verdict: **the suspected defect is FALSIFIED for `motir-gateway`.** No behaviour change.

The card asked for the measurement first and said both outcomes were legal. The measurement says the gateway's Neon compute **does** suspend between syncs, so `SYNC_FREQUENCY` stays at **600**.

## The measurement

Neon's control plane sampled every **20 s** — tighter than the card's 30 s deliberately, because the predicted idle window was short enough that 30 s could alias it — with **no database connection of the run's own**, so the probe cannot wake what it measures.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| endpoint | `ep-crimson-dew-ai3vmlx0`, Neon project `autumn-sky-90851862` (`name: motir-gateway`) |
| window | **2026-08-23 20:48:11Z → 21:33:03Z** (44m52s), 133 samples |
| API traffic in window | **zero**, verified in `fly logs` — the two sync goroutines were the only thing touching Postgres |
| wakes (endpoint `last_active`) | 20:45:28 · 20:55:29 · 21:05:31 · 21:15:22 · 21:25:23 |
| wake intervals | **601, 602, 591, 601 s** — each matching a `syncing options from database` log line |
| suspend delay | **~5m12s**, bounded **4m46s – 5m37s**, five consecutive cycles |
| duty cycle | **53.4% awake** (71 of 133 samples) · **46.6% asleep** |

Per cycle: awake ~310 s, asleep ~290 s. **600 s clears the real delay by about five minutes, not by one.** The gateway is not the third copy of the `motir-ai` defect.

### Traffic accounting — and one confound that was mine

The window is traffic-free, but earlier requests in the same log were not incidental. Gateway relay traffic at 19:54:07, 19:56:18, 19:58:07 and 20:19:03 each landed within seconds of an MCP **content** write of my own, embedding `text-embedding-3-small` through the `motir-ai-planner` token — motir-core → motir-ai → the gateway. Status-only transitions produced none.

That is a contamination path worth stating plainly, because I had reasoned the opposite at the start of the run: *"MCP calls hit `app.motir.co`, which is motir-core's Neon project, so they cannot touch this measurement."* They can, one hop further out. The clean window opens at **20:19:04** and the sampled window sits entirely inside it.

## The finding that outlives the card

§21 records the suspend delay as **~9 minutes**, measured 2026-08-20 by the same method on two sibling endpoints. Three days later this endpoint gives **~5 minutes**, consistently over five cycles — and **nothing in our configuration explains the gap**. Read from the platform on 2026-08-23, all four projects in the org carry the identical `suspend_timeout_seconds: 0` and the same `0.25 – 8` CU autoscale:

```
motir-core     snowy-truth-13928044      ep_suspend=0   autoscale 0.25-8
motir-gateway  autumn-sky-90851862       ep_suspend=0   autoscale 0.25-8
motir-ai       hidden-thunder-40380051   ep_suspend=0   autoscale 0.25-8
taq            odd-silence-89227746      ep_suspend=0   autoscale 0.25-8
```

So the card's own thesis survives in a stronger form than it was written: *an interval is only ever as good as the threshold it clears* — and **a threshold from measurement is not a contract either.** It is a reading with a date on it, and this one moved four minutes in three days.

**Whether that is a per-endpoint difference or a platform change is NOT settled here.** This card measured one endpoint and says so. Re-measuring `motir-ai`'s and `taq`'s endpoints would settle it and is a separate card's work.

## What was deliberately NOT done

- **`SYNC_FREQUENCY` is unchanged at 600.** Criterion 2 makes the disposition follow the measurement, and the measurement falsifies the premise.
- **Raising it to 1800 was considered and rejected as out of scope.** It would buy roughly another ~$7/mo (83% asleep instead of 47%) at the cost of admin edits taking up to 30 min to propagate. That is a new trade the card did not authorise, and it belongs in its own card rather than being folded in under a falsified premise. Flagged for Yue, not decided here.
- **No upstream file was touched.** `UPSTREAM.md` states the Motir layer is *"intentionally kept OUTSIDE the upstream tree (`NOTICE`, `UPSTREAM.md`, `fly.toml`, `motir/`)"*. Fix option 1 — delete the poll, invalidate on write — would have modified `model/option.go` and `model/cache.go`, where our fork is currently **byte-identical to upstream** (`songquanpeng/one-api`, checked at `SyncOptions` and `SyncChannelCache`). That is the rebase-survival argument the card asked for, and it is moot here anyway since nothing needed fixing.

## How to test

Not a rendered surface, and there is no behaviour to exercise — the diff is comments and a documentation section. To re-take the measurement:

```
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat ~/.config/neon/api-key-org)" \
  https://console.neon.tech/api/v2/projects/autumn-sky-90851862/endpoints
```

Sample `current_state` / `last_active` on a loop, with no database connection, over a window you can show was traffic-free in `fly logs -a motir-gateway`.

author: zacharyzcr
body:
Answers the census request in #594: @mfethe1 verified our framing algebra against their VQ3R record geometry from the published spec alone, and asked for per-record rows — `{record_id, logical_bytes, encoded_payload_bytes, framing_bytes, physical_offset, physical_extent_bytes, alignment_bytes}` — to check for hidden byte amplification on real data rather than the achieved-ratio average.

`repack_rans.py --census <dir>` now produces exactly that, read-only, to `rans-census.json`, with a per-shard summary line (logical/encoded/framed sums and the framing percentage). Semantics pinned in the code so the numbers are comparable across formats; the one field that needed a decision is `alignment_bytes`: **0 by construction** in this layout — records pack back to back in the safetensors data section, and O_DIRECT alignment is the reader's page window, not a property of the stored bytes. A cross-format table wants that as an explicit zero, not a missing column.

Accounting is enforced, not assumed: any record whose extent is not exactly `round16(header) + payload + round16 pad` fails the run with an `UNATTRIBUTED_BYTES` row. The new test pins full attribution against the synthetic fixture corpus (9/9 suite green).

No wire-format change, no re-encoding — sidecar tooling only, same family as `--manifest-only`.

body:
Combines #2759, #2769, #2770, #2771 and #2772 into a single PR (those are now closed in favor of this one), plus further script additions on top. This PR is being extended incrementally - each script lands as its own commit directly on this branch, with the PR description updated as it grows.

## What

LibreCAD ships two LFF fonts - `standard.lff` (the default) and `unicode.lff` (the widest script coverage). Both had real gaps: `standard.lff` had no Turkish-specific characters, and `unicode.lff` had zero or partial coverage for most non-Latin scripts. A missing glyph is not loud - `RS_Text`/`RS_MText` silently substitute the U+FFFD replacement diamond for any unresolved codepoint - so the gap just quietly renders wrong instead of erroring. The goal is full coverage of every living-language script except CJK (Chinese/Japanese/Korean Han-based scripts are a different scale of effort - thousands of characters - and explicitly out of scope).

| 21 | Greek base block completion (+ Coptic-in-Greek-block letters) | `bc9dfc63f` | 60 | Greek, ~13M, official (Greece/Cyprus); Coptic liturgical/Egyptological use | No |
| 22 | Ethiopic Extended-A | `439fdd04b` | 32 | Gurage languages: Silt'e ~1M, Wolane, Zay (Ethiopia) | No |
| 23 | Old Church Slavonic liturgical letters | `f88aafc5f` | 34 | Church Slavonic, printed today in Russian Orthodox liturgical texts | No |
| 24 | Greek Extended (polytonic) | `ead51acd6` | 233 | Ancient/Koine Greek, actively taught and published today | No |
| 25 | Modern minority-language Cyrillic extensions | `95dc8d2a4` | 194 | Abkhaz/Komi/Khakas/Kildin Sami/Aleut/Nanai/Even/Khanty/Mansi/Caucasian minority languages | No |

`unicode.lff` glyph count: 2693 → 6543 (+3850) so far. `standard.lff` gains its 6 Turkish characters.

At this point the original script-by-script sweep gave way to a second, deeper survey (Greek and Cyrillic coverage gaps specifically, plus any other living scripts missed the first time) - see below for what that turned up and what's still to come. Greek (row 21) was the first result of that survey: the base 0370-03FF block was only 71/135 codepoints covered before this - the everyday alphabet was there, but the archaic letters, symbol-form variants, two punctuation marks, and the 14 Coptic letters historically encoded in the Greek block were all missing. Ethiopic Extended-A (row 22) fills the Gurage-language syllables the original Ethiopic commit didn't cover - same tractability, same reference font. Old Church Slavonic (row 23) turned out to need scoping down from the original estimate: the well-defined liturgical core (0x0460-0x0481, 17 letter pairs still printed in Church Slavonic service books today) is what's covered here, with the rest of that territory picked up in row 25. Greek Extended (row 24), the biggest single item from the survey, is all 233 codepoints of the systematic breathing/accent/iota-subscript combination space that polytonic (Ancient/Koine) Greek needs, verified in family-grouped batches (alpha/epsilon/eta/iota/omicron/upsilon/omega) plus the usual pairwise-duplicate check, which found one pair (koronis/psili) that's a genuine font design choice, not a bug - confirmed by comparing raw rasterized pixels, not just traced output. Row 25 closes out the modern minority-language Cyrillic cluster flagged as future work back at row 23 - the rest of the extended Cyrillic range (0x048A-0x0527 and Cyrillic Extended-B) covering Abkhaz, Komi, Khakas, Kildin Sami, Aleut, several Siberian/Far-Eastern languages, Caucasian minority languages, and the remaining genuine Old Cyrillic paleographic letters (including the famous 7-circle Multiocular O). Its one pairwise duplicate (palochka/small-palochka) is the same kind of genuine font-design-choice finding as Greek's koronis/psili.

This closes out essentially everything identified across both surveys, aside from the SMP-blocked scripts documented above as a core-engine gap.

**Not attempted - a separate rendering-engine limitation, not a font-data problem**: Wancho, Mro, Osage, Warang Citi and Sora Sompeng are all otherwise-tractable alphabets (no shaping needed), but their codepoints sit above U+FFFF (Unicode's Supplementary Multilingual Plane). `unicode.lff`'s own parser already handles this correctly (`RS_Font::extractFontChar` was widened to 6 hex digits / `char32_t` in an earlier, unrelated fix), but `RS_Text::update()` and `RS_MText`'s segment-building/`addLetter` both iterate text by `QChar` (one UTF-16 code unit) rather than by full codepoint - so a surrogate pair gets split into two separate failed font lookups, and the character renders as two U+FFFD placeholder boxes even with perfectly correct glyph data present. (`RS_MText` already self-documents this exact gap in a comment at rs_mtext.cpp:766-772.) Fixing it is a real, scoped core-engine change - detect and consume surrogate pairs as one unit before font lookup, in both entities - but it's a text-rendering fix, not something a font-only PR should carry silently. Flagging it here in case it's worth a follow-up issue.

author: camshaft
body:
Fixes a real bug blocking the natural reducer authoring form, found while debugging v-syntax's + v-platform's flagship-reducer repros.

**Bug:** the no-redeclare sidecar's `top_level_items` only recognized a `(module NAME item…)` or bare root — **not** a `(do item…)` root. But a bare source file with no `(module)` wrapper parses to a `(do …)` root (and that's what v-syntax's ML surface renders to). So an in-source `(world …)` in a `(do)`-rooted program was **invisible**: the world wasn't found, nothing was synthesized, and every world import cascaded to `CDZ0101 unbound`.

**Fix:** add a `(do …)` arm to `top_level_items` (return the do's items), mirroring `proptest_gen` / `param_sidecar`, which already treat a `(do)` root as the top-level item list.

**Test** `a_do_rooted_reducer_synthesizes_its_in_source_world_import_effects`: a `(do (world …) (def on-message …performing identity.id…) (export …))` reducer now binds `identity` + lowers to a `HostCall`. Verified via `cdz check`: **unbound before, clean after**.

**Safety:** no-op for `(do)` roots with no world; `(module)`/artifact paths unchanged. Full `rcdzc` lib **2738/0**; clippy `-D warnings` + pinned fmt clean; only `wit_world.rs` + `tests.rs`.

Related: two of the three repros I received were actually **malformed WIT descriptors** (`Bytes` written in a world descriptor position, where WIT wants `("list" (u8))`) — caught by the malformed-world diagnostic in #3116 (pending). And v-platform's **external-artifact** "unbound" does **not** reproduce on current main — it now binds (only the backend `list<u8>`-result declines, v-rb's residual), so that was a stale-binary artifact.

## Problem
When closing the currently active tab on mobile, the app clears the selection instead of switching to a recently active tab, losing user context and requiring manual tab selection.

## Solution
Track tab activation recency (max 100 tabs) and restore to the most recent surviving tab when the active tab closes, unless the user selected a different tab during the close request. Handles edge cases like tabs omitted in snapshots, terminal creation during flight, and racing selections.

## What Changed
New module `mobile-session-tab-recency.ts` with recency tracking and selection logic. Session screen now maintains refs for recent tab history and selection revision counter. Increments counter on tab switches, terminal creation, and host updates to distinguish user interaction from auto-selection. Updated close handler to pick the previous tab instead of clearing, unless user changed selection mid-close.

Fixed a race condition where terminals created while a close was pending could be lost by updating sessionTabsRef before React state commit.

## Summary

Screen of the **Antianginals** subsection (Cardiovascular Drugs) — **6 drug entries** + **35 flashcards** — against **BNF, NICE (NG185/CG126 stable angina, NG106 HF), NHS**. Screened via 4 parallel reviewers (2 drug groups + 2 flashcard halves).

The content was strong. Two minor accuracy fixes.

## Fixes

**1. Ranolazine — hepatic contraindication threshold.** Listed *"severe hepatic or renal impairment."* BNF contraindicates ranolazine in **moderate-to-severe hepatic impairment** (not only severe). Corrected to *"moderate-to-severe hepatic impairment, severe renal impairment (CrCl <30)."*

**2. Trimetazidine — regulator attribution (drug note + flashcard 34).** The second-line-only restriction was attributed to the **MHRA** (drug pearl, a contraindication parenthetical, and flashcard 34). The 2012 restriction was an **EMA Article 31 referral**; trimetazidine has no UK marketing authorisation, so the MHRA did not independently restrict it. - **Ranolazine** — late-Na-current inhibition, QT/CYP3A4 profile. **Trimetazidine** — metabolic modulator + the movement-disorder/parkinsonism caution.

author: rickymarino-priv
body:
Segunda rebanada de Fase 0. El alta de un municipio por API crea su base de datos propia, la migra, la siembra y recién ahí lo activa.

## Demo

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/admin/municipios \
  -H "X-Admin-Token: cambiar-en-r3" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"slug":"sanmartin","nombreMunicipio":"San Martín", ...}'
```

Después de eso, `sanmartin.localhost:5173` muestra el portal con su marca **y sus datos de contacto leídos de `tenant_sanmartin`**, no de la base de control.

## Decisiones que vale la pena mirar

**Dos unidades de persistencia.** La base de control y las de municipio tienen esquemas distintos, así que necesitan `EntityManagerFactory` separados; el reparto es por paquete. Un único EMF sobre el datasource ruteado no podría validar ningún esquema.

**El datasource de tenants falla si no hay municipio resuelto.** No hay valor por defecto: sería escribir los datos de un municipio en la base de otro.

**La persistencia quedó en su propio módulo.** Spring Modulith detectó un ciclo entre el paquete raíz y `tenants`; moverla deja la dependencia en un solo sentido.

**Los municipios ya no se siembran por migración.** Se crean por la API, que es como se crean de verdad — los tests usan ese mismo camino, con creación de base real.

## Provisorio, a reemplazar en R3

La API de administración es cross-tenant y la autenticación llega recién en R3. Dejarla abierta sería un agujero, no hardening diferido, así que la protege un token de configuración. **No alcanza como solución final**: un token compartido no identifica a nadie, y ADR 0009 pide poder auditar quién dio de alta o suspendió un municipio.

## Verificación

- 14/14 tests en verde, incluidos los de aislamiento entre municipios y el de límites entre módulos.
- Verificado en el navegador: dos municipios dados de alta por API, cada uno mostrando los datos de su propia base.
- Verificado en la base: `tenant_sanmartin` y `tenant_moron` existen por separado y cada una tiene solo sus datos.

## Summary

author: liamriddell
body:
Fixes #175.

Typing `\`, or any line built only from characters the lexer discards, showed a result of **0** in the notepad and the playground: a number on screen for a line that holds no expression, where a blank line, a heading and a prose line all show nothing.

## Cause

The lexer classifies any unknown ASCII character as `CharClass.SKIP` and discards it, the same path whitespace takes, so a line built only from them tokenises to an empty token stream. The line was still classified as an `expression` and evaluated, and the engine reports an empty token stream as the number `0`.

## Fix

One change, at the shared classifier. `classifyFromPositions` now recognises a line whose every character is discarded by the tokeniser (ASCII whitespace or a skip character) as empty, the same as a blank line. That single classification is what the batch parse (`parseDocument`), the incremental evaluator, and the playground's prose gate (`shouldEvaluateLine` → `classifyLine`) all read, so every surface skips such a line rather than answering 0.

```
\           was 0, now no result
\          was 0, now no result
\\        was 0, now no result
```

## Boundary

A backslash next to real content is unchanged: `\1` is still `1` (the backslash is skipped), and `1 \ 2` still errors on the trailing `2`. A non-ASCII code point stays real content (it lexes as an `IDENT` for forward compatibility), so a line of accented or CJK text is untouched.

## Verification

- New regression spec `Issue175_backslashOnlyLineEmpty.spec.ts` (11 cases): `classifyLine` marks the line empty, `parseDocument` reports no result and no error, and the boundary cases (`\1`, `1 \ 2`, a blank line, a real expression) hold.
- Full serial gate green: **7,689 passed across 336 suites**, no failures. Comment-style, oxlint, `lint:size` and `lint:stats` all current (test stats regenerated to 7,694/336; package size to 125,164 bytes gzipped).

body:
## Summary

Adds an application-provided **DataStore storage adapter** so AutoMobile's storage inspection covers apps that keep preferences in [Jetpack DataStore](https://developer.android.com/topic/libraries/architecture/datastore) rather than conventional `SharedPreferences` files. Previously DataStore state could only be inferred from implementation-specific files; this introduces an explicit, read-only, lifecycle-safe adapter contract instead.

The SDK never links against `androidx.datastore` — the host implements `DataStoreAdapter` against its own DataStore instances and registers it by a stable name. Read-only enforcement, redaction, and capability reporting all live at the AutoMobile boundary, independent of the host implementation.

## Linked Issue

Progresses #5192 — delivers the SDK-side DataStore adapter contract and the debug `ContentProvider` surface. Full end-to-end reach through the MCP tool → CtrlProxy → provider chain is tracked in #5573 (it requires runner-protocol wiring + an Android control-proxy release re-cut). #5192 stays open until #5573 lands.

## Changes

- **`DataStoreAdapter`** — host-provided, read-only integration contract (`suspend storeNames()` / `read()`); no filesystem paths, no mutation entry point, cooperative cancellation.
- **`DataStoreInspector`** — lifecycle-safe registry (register/replace/`unregisterAdapter`/`reset`) with boundary-enforced read-only mode, a configurable `DataStoreRedactionPolicy`, and `capabilities()` reporting. `reset()` wired into `AutoMobileSDK.shutdown()`.
- **Structured models & errors** — `DataStoreDescriptor` (name + entryCount, no path), `DataStoreEntry`, `DataStoreValueType` (incl. `DOUBLE`, `BYTE_ARRAY`, `UNKNOWN`); `AdapterNotFound` / `StoreNotFound` / `ReadError` / `UnsupportedValue`.
- **Existing surface wiring** — `listDataStores` / `getDataStore` added to the debug storage `ContentProvider`, reusing the existing `StorageResponse` shapes (no shared/runner protocol change; path emitted empty).
- **`FakeDataStoreAdapter`** reference/fake for deterministic tests.
- **Docs** — DataStore integration contract and limitations in the Android SDK design doc.

## Validation

- [x] Android changes: ran the matching `scripts/` validation (`scripts/ktfmt/validate_ktfmt.sh` clean tree-wide)
- [x] `:auto-mobile-sdk:testDebugUnitTest` full module suite green; `:auto-mobile-sdk:detekt` green
- [x] New code uses interfaces + fakes; unit tests run in <100ms
- [x] No new dependency (adapter is a pure host-provided contract)
- [ ] TypeScript checks N/A — no TS/schema surfaces touched

## Kotlin Reuse Check

- [x] Mirrors the existing `SharedPreferencesInspector` / `DatabaseInspector` registry pattern and reuses existing `StorageResponse` protocol types rather than adding new ones; no new helpers/`*Util` files or dependencies.
- [x] Read-only by contract: the interface exposes no mutation method, so read-only is structural rather than a flag the host must honor.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] Host can register a DataStore adapter without exposing filesystem paths (`DataStoreDescriptor` has no path member).
- [~] DataStore-backed preferences discoverable & readable through the storage **ContentProvider** surface (`listDataStores`/`getDataStore`, via `adb shell content call`). End-to-end MCP/CtrlProxy reach deferred to #5573.
- [x] Stores, keys, values, and unsupported value types have structured representations and errors.
- [x] Read-only mode and configured redaction enforced at the AutoMobile boundary.
- [x] Registration, replacement, and removal are lifecycle-safe; no leaked listeners/coroutines (reads run in caller context; `shutdown()` clears adapters).
- [x] Documentation covers the integration contract and limitations.
- [x] Tests cover a preferences DataStore fake, missing stores, malformed values, shutdown, and cancellation.


## Follow-ups

- #5573 — expose the DataStore adapter through the end-to-end MCP storage surface (runner wiring + release re-cut).

author: patcireamo
body:
`getNextSiblingIndex` answered "what index does the next child of this parent take" from a query filtered on the parent and nothing else:

```sql
SELECT MAX(sibling_index) FROM messages WHERE parent_id IS ?
```

For a real parent that is harmless, since message ids are unique and every child of one is necessarily in the same chat. For a root it is not: every chat's roots carry a NULL parent, so the query swept root rows across the entire install. Reproduced against a throwaway database: with one chat holding a root at index 12, a brand new chat's first root came back as 13.

## Why it was worth repairing

**It is latent, not live.** Every reader sorts by the value rather than reading it as a position, and the one number a reader ever sees ("Variant N of M") is derived from position in the sorted list, never from the stored value. An inflated index still sorts last among its own siblings, so nothing on screen was ever wrong.

Two things make it worth closing anyway. Unrelated chats must not number each other's rows at all, and the number grew without bound across an install. And a second reading of it already exists: `mirrorsGreetings` requires `sibling_index === i`, a position. The two rules cannot currently meet, because every path that inflates a root index also adds or removes a root row and so trips the row-count gate first, but that is a coincidence of today's call graph rather than a guarantee.

## The change

The question carries the chat now. That is a signature change across the client/server RPC boundary, so it touches the server method, the client proxy and six call sites. The RPC allowlist keys on the method name rather than its arity, so it needed no edit.

`nextRootSiblingIndex` goes with it. That pure helper existed only because the db could not be trusted for roots, and its one caller was pulling a whole transcript over the wire to feed it a single number. Its four cases move into `server/siblingIndex.test.ts` and now run against real SQL.

## Stored data

**No migration.** The function returns `MAX + 1` over exactly the sibling set it is about to insert into, so the result is strictly greater than every member of that set whatever is already in there. The old query was simply wider than the insert set, which is why the bug never corrupted anything; the fix narrows it to the set it is actually about. Both are collision-free. Inflated values already on disk stay legal: they are an ordering, and gaps were always normal (a deleted greeting leaves one).

## Query cost

`EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` shows the new clause served by the existing `idx_messages_chat`. Measured on 40 chats and 7,340 rows with one chat holding 5,000 turns, the worst case is ~0.2 ms, once per turn, next to an LLM round trip of seconds. A composite `(chat_id, parent_id)` index would restore an exact seek but needs a schema migration to buy back a fifth of a millisecond, so it is not here.

## Notes

`architecture/chat-sessions.md` and `architecture/testing.md` move with the code. `bun test` (1036 pass) and `bun run check` are clean, and the new tests were confirmed to fail against the old query.

Found in passing and deliberately left alone: the schema permits a row whose parent lives in another chat (nothing produces one, and chat duplication throws rather than copying one silently). Closing it means a `CHECK` or a trigger, so it belongs to the next change that touches the schema for its own reasons rather than to this one.

author: ralphhtml
body:
Two problems, one fix.

The app's own colours are red, and a lot of panels had been written at different times in dark navy, so Settings and half the overlays looked like they belonged to a different application. And every surface was a single flat colour, which reads as a rectangle painted on the map rather than a thing sitting on top of it.

## The surface system

One block of CSS holding a small set of gradient tokens, applied by name to every surface in the app:

| Token | What it is |
|---|---|
| `--grad-panel` | a panel shell |
| `--grad-surface` | a card inside one |
| `--grad-card` | a row inside a card |
| `--grad-raise` | something to press |
| `--grad-sunk` | something already pressed, or cut in |
| `--grad-scrim` | the dim behind a modal |
| `--edge-3d` | inset highlight along the top lip, shadow along the bottom |
| `--lift-3d` | the drop, so the slab has somewhere to sit |

That inset pair is the whole 3D effect, and it costs nothing to draw.

**Direction carries meaning.** A button is lit from above. A slider track, a toggle track and a text field are lit from below, so they read as cut into the panel rather than laid on it. A selected tab swaps from card to raised, so the rail no longer reads as one block.

These set `background-image` rather than `background`. A gradient is an image and an image paints above the background colour, so this layers over what each panel already declared without fighting a hundred existing rules — several of them `!important` — one at a time.

## What it covers

25 panel shells, 6 scrims, the cards inside them, map bubbles and pills, every Leaflet popup **and its tip** (the tip matters, or the little arrow hangs off the corner in a different colour), the right-click menu, tooltips, all nine toolbars, the top search bar, the attribution and scale controls, the cyclone ensemble and the sounding panel (both still in navy), the drawing tools down the right edge, and the animation bar, which was a solid cyan strip across the bottom of a red application.

A pop-out panel is a separate document that the page's stylesheet does not reach, so `_popCss` carries its own copy. A pinned window that looks like a different app from the panel it came out of is the problem this was meant to solve.

## One regression the change caused, and fixes

`#timeline-labels` was pure black, which read fine on the cyan the animation bar used to be and not at all on the red it is now.

## Tests

`tools/test-surface-system.mjs`, 34 checks. It does not read the CSS and take its word for it: it opens the page, finds the surfaces in the real DOM and asks the browser what it computed. Panels built lazily are measured through a stand-in with the same id, so a selector typo cannot hide behind an absent element.

Every surface is asserted to be a gradient **and** to be red. The last section is a real contrast ratio over each stop of each background — that is what caught the black tick labels, and it is verified to fail again when they are put back.

All JS suites pass: borders 42, gestures 23, alert desk 76, pop-out 37, audit 17, settings/graphics/JTWC 35, map-menu 46, radar fx 85, load budget 29.

## Note

The Sign In chip and the Asturio button keep their blue rings. Red is the main colour; a couple of deliberate accents are what stop everything reading as one flat sheet. Say the word if you want those in red too.

author: oichkatzelesfrettschen
body:
T7.1 of the P7 graphics ladder: object lifetime completeness for buffer, image, view, sampler, and binding.

Mechanism: VkSampler becomes recorded state (creation depends on no format or route; use stays fail-closed at the descriptor write, which poisons the set and refuses the dispatch recording; enabled anisotropy refuses -- the feature is withheld). VkBufferView keeps its refusal, now grounded in the advertised format table (buffer features are VERTEX_BUFFER alone, so no valid create exists). vkBindBufferMemory2/vkBindImageMemory gain the full once-only admission: null handles, rebind, page misalignment, footprint past the allocation end, and the CPU-inaccessible memory type all refuse before any state change.

Consumers repaired: the loader sweep expects the sampler to construct and destroy; the compute GPU-route alias arm binds its aliased buffer at a page-aligned offset (the reported alignment), keeping the disjoint-range one-BO shape the arm tests.

Validation: debug-optimized -Dwerror build clean; suites r3v/r300/radeon-drm-vk/drm-shim under env -u R3V_NATIVE_MANIFEST_DIR = 286 OK / 34 xfail / 0 fail / 21 skipped (replay-gated tests without the kernel-tool env). New test r3v-native-object-lifetime plus two should_fail known-bad arms (rebind admitted, wrong-type bind admitted) run green.

Assisted-by: Claude (Fable 5)

## Summary by Sourcery

Complete the R3V native object-lifetime contract for samplers, buffer views, buffers, and images.

New Features:
- Support recorded-state sampler creation and destruction while keeping sampler use fail-closed.
- Add complete validation for one-time buffer and image memory binding admission.
- Add native object-lifetime coverage for samplers, buffer views, and memory bindings, including known-bad mutation checks.

Bug Fixes:
- Align the compute GPU-route alias allocation and binding to the required page boundary.

Enhancements:
- Update native entrypoint and loader audits to reflect the sampler's live lifecycle contract.

Tests:
- Add drm-shim coverage for sampler lifetime, buffer-view refusal, and valid and invalid buffer/image memory bindings.

author: codeconsole
body:
Two settings for the MongoDB index build that runs when the datastore starts, plus the reporting to make either decision an informed one.

All of these are runtime configuration, set in `grails-app/conf/application.yml` (or `application.groovy`) — nothing in `build.gradle`.

## `grails.mongodb.buildIndexes`

```yaml
grails:
    mongodb:
        buildIndexes: false
```

GORM creates and reconciles every index declared in a mapping block each time the datastore starts, with no way to switch it off. That is unwanted when deploying against live data whose indexes are managed separately, by a DBA or a migration step: the deployment builds indexes against production collections and reconciles the index set the running application depends on.

With the setting off, no `createIndex` or `collMod` is issued for any domain class and the indexes on the server are left exactly as they are. Persistence and querying are unaffected and keep using whichever indexes exist. It also covers domain classes registered after startup, and resolves per connection like every other connection setting, so index building can be switched off globally and left on for one connection:

```yaml
grails:
    mongodb:
        buildIndexes: false
        connections:
            reporting:
                url: mongodb://localhost/reporting
                buildIndexes: true
```

A collection that has never started up with index building enabled will have no declared indexes at all, so this is for environments where the indexes are already in place or are applied by other means. It governs only what GORM derives from mapping blocks; an explicit `createIndex` in application code is unaffected.

## `grails.mongodb.buildIndexesAsync`

```yaml
grails:
    mongodb:
        buildIndexesAsync: true
```

MongoDB answers a `createIndex` only once the index has been built, so by default startup waits for every declared index in turn. Measured against MongoDB 7.0 with 200k documents: 172ms to create one index on the calling thread, 1.2ms to re-issue the same declaration. `background: true` has been ignored since MongoDB 4.2 and costs the same.

With this enabled the startup build runs on one daemon thread per connection, named `gorm-mongo-index-build-<connection>`, and startup continues without waiting. Indexes are still built one at a time rather than all at once against the server.

Worth planning for:

- A query issued before its index has been built is served without it — correctly, but unindexed. A `unique` index likewise constrains nothing until the build finishes.
- Startup no longer waits, so a failed index build can no longer fail startup. It is logged at error level and the application runs without that index. The default synchronous build still propagates the exception.
- It applies to the startup build only. A domain class registered afterwards is indexed on the thread registering it, which keeps the tenant context that path can depend on.

## Index build reporting

A successful build previously logged nothing at all — only conflicts, TTL updates and failures — so there was no way to tell how much of startup went on indexes, and with the async build no signal that it had finished. It now logs one summary:

```
Index build for database [myDb] finished in 412ms: 2 created, 5 already present, from 3 domain class(es)
```

The created/already-present split is what makes the elapsed time interpretable: a restart that changed no mappings reports everything as already present and costs milliseconds, so a summary reporting indexes created is the one that accounts for a slow start. A build with failures is logged at `WARN` and reports how many. Each index also logs its own elapsed time at `DEBUG` under `org.grails.datastore.mapping.core`, which is how to find the single slow index behind a slow summary.

`createIndexes` reports `numIndexesBefore` / `numIndexesAfter`, but the driver's `createIndex` helper discards the response and returns only the index name. Rather than hand-roll the command — the `IndexOptions` to index-specification mapping is not worth reimplementing — the build lists the indexes a collection already has. That listing is lazy, so an entity declaring no indexes costs no round trip, and it replaces the listing the conflict path used to make for itself. If it cannot be read, the build still runs and the summary falls back to reporting how many declarations were applied.

## Settings were ignored when the application supplies its own `MongoClient`

Found while testing the above. The constructors taking a `MongoClient` (or a `MongoClientSettings.Builder`) built the default connection source from a bare `MongoConnectionSourceSettings`, so every `grails.mongodb` setting describing how the datastore behaves — `stateless`, `transactional`, `engine`, flush mode, `decimalType`, and now `buildIndexes` — was silently left at its default. Only `databaseName` survived, because it is set explicitly from the mapping context.

That path is not obscure: Spring Boot's MongoDB auto-configuration contributes a `MongoClient` bean and `MongoDbGormAutoConfiguration` hands that client to GORM whenever one is present, so a Spring Boot application configuring GORM through `grails.mongodb` was being ignored. The settings are now bound from the configuration on that path too; the connection details in them go unused, as the client arrives already connected.

This is a behaviour change for anyone who had been running on defaults without knowing it — a `stateless = true` or `transactional = true` that was previously discarded now takes effect.

## Notes

- Documented in `grails-data-mongodb/docs` under Querying Indexing and Advanced Configuration, with the 8.0 release notes updated. Those pages showed configuration only in the `application.groovy` DSL, so they now show the `application.yml` form as well, and note that these settings are read by name — they are not relaxed-bound like Spring Boot's own properties, so a kebab-case spelling such as `build-indexes` is ignored and leaves the default in place.
- The mongo core tests now run against logback rather than the no-op SLF4J binding, as `grails-data-neo4j/core` already does, so a test can assert on what was logged. The root logger is pinned to `WARN` by a `logback-test.xml`, and the build output is unchanged.

author: prosefairplaymediation
body:
A push protocol rather than waiting for a re-crawl: the site tells Bing what
changed. Yandex, Naver and Seznam share the same endpoint, so one POST reaches
all four. Google does not participate.

**Why it matters here specifically:** Bing's index is what ChatGPT's web search
leans on, so this shortens the gap between publishing and being answerable in
ChatGPT from days to hours.

## Three pieces

- **`public/680bede00d26f37ea47d4561099c5093.txt`** — proves ownership. Contains
  the bare key with no trailing newline, which is what the protocol wants.
- **`scripts/indexnow.mjs`** — reads URLs from the built sitemap rather than a
  hand-kept list, so a new page is submitted the moment it ships. It fetches
  the key file first and **refuses to submit if it's missing or wrong**: a 404
  there is the difference between "submitted" and "silently rejected".
- **`.github/workflows/indexnow.yml`** — runs on pushes to `main` touching
  `src/`, `public/` or the Astro config. A README edit changes nothing a
  crawler sees, so it doesn't trigger. Waits three minutes first so Cloudflare
  has finished deploying — otherwise the submission points crawlers at the
  previous build.

## Verification

- Key file ships to `dist` with exactly the key as its contents (32 bytes, no
  newline).
- Sitemap extraction finds all 30 URLs.
- Key file correctly absent from the sitemap itself.

## Not run here

The live submission needs the key file reachable at
`https://prosefairplaymediation.com/…`, which it won't be until this merges and
Cloudflare deploys. First real run happens on the next content push, or
manually from the Actions tab.

author: 1357aiworkspace-code
body:
## Problem
Cascade can still show a short black flash during effect-heavy chained clears, especially consecutive stripe activations. The player also reports occasional apparent page reloads and a mostly-black browser failure surface with a gray exclamation mark.

## Reproduction and evidence
- add a dedicated headed Chromium/Xvfb compositor lane
- force full motion/full effects and repeatedly overlap nuclear clear phases
- capture Chrome compositor frames and inspect the particle canvas source separately
- detect renderer crashes, unexpected main-document navigations/reloads, board disappearance, canvas context loss, and compositor-layer runaway
- A/B testing isolated the layer explosion to overlapping DOM juice effects, not the 360-particle canvas:
  - uncapped combined stress: roughly 600 compositor layers
  - DOM juice hidden: roughly 28 layers
  - 240-node prototype: roughly 250 layers
  - newest-28 effect-group guard: 185 layers in the measured headed run
- the particle path still reaches the full 360-particle budget

## Fix
- keep the newest 28 top-level DOM effect groups painted; older fading generations stop painting once a newer cascade phase arrives
- preserve the complete current maximum-strength phase plus a small amount of overlap
- do not reduce the 360-particle spectacle
- add persistent Cascade renderer lifecycle breadcrumbs so a real-device restart can distinguish:
  - normal pagehide
  - intentional session-revalidation reload
  - intentional build-update reload
  - Chromium page discard
  - recent abrupt document loss with the last recorded VFX pressure
- tag GameFrame session-revalidation reloads explicitly
- include the new assets in the installed/offline cache and advance the cache version

## Regression coverage
- headed compositor must survive stacked nuclear clears without black frames, crash, reload, context loss, board hiding, or layer runaway
- guarded rendering is compared directly against legacy uncapped rendering
- lifecycle tests prove abrupt-recovery, intentional-reload, and clean-pagehide classification

The CI compositor cannot yet reproduce the literal hardware black frame, so this PR does not claim that exact pixel failure has been captured. It does reproduce and remove the remaining cross-transition compositor-pressure defect and adds on-device evidence collection for any future actual renderer restart.

author: tylerkron
body:
Produced by the DUPLICATE-UNIFIER maintenance routine. Safe because the extracted helper is the same three lines both callers already ran, and nothing about the bytes on the wire changes.

**What was wrong.** `Pic32BootloaderMessageConsumer` decodes the bootloader's bare acknowledgment frame — `SOH <opcode>`, no payload — in two places. `DecodeProgramFlashResponse` and `DecodeEraseFlashResponse` were byte-for-byte identical apart from the opcode each compares against:

```csharp
if (data.Length < 2) return false;
if (data[0] != StartOfHeader) return false;
return data[1] == ProgramFlashCommand;   // ...or EraseFlashCommand
```

The two are not merely similar, they *have* to agree: the erase ack and the program ack are the same wire frame, so any change to how one is framed applies to the other. Split across two copies, a fix to one is a silent divergence from the other, and the failure would not be loud — it would be a live flash session mis-reading an acknowledgment on real hardware. The class's own doc comment already argues this case for the opcodes ("shared ... so the two sides cannot drift apart"); the rule that reads them was still written down twice.

**How it was fixed.** One private `IsAckFor(byte[] data, byte command)` now holds the framing rule; both public methods become expression-bodied one-liners passing their own opcode. Public signatures, return values, and behavior are unchanged.

The one thing worth pushing back on, so I'll raise it myself: the helper does **not** null-guard `data`, even though the file's `DecodeReadCrcResponse` does guard its input. That is on purpose. Both callers are public methods that have always thrown `NullReferenceException` on null, and adding `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull` in the shared helper would change that observable behavior for both of them — a behavior change smuggled into a refactor that claims to have none. The helper carries a comment saying so. The underlying inconsistency (one of four decoders on this type null-guards, three don't) is real and is filed separately as #621; this PR does not settle it either way.

**Divergence check: none.** The two copies agreed exactly. So a straight unification was correct, with no behavior to choose between.

**Verified.** `dotnet build` 0 warnings / 0 errors. Full `dotnet test` green on net9.0 and net10.0 — 3762 passed, 0 failed, 2 pre-existing skips per TFM, plus 217 in Daqifi.Mcp.Tests. Added one theory, `BadlyFramedAcknowledgment_IsRejectedByBothAckDecoders`: the existing tests asserted each decoder's rejection cases independently, so nothing pinned the half the two share — the property the extraction exists to guarantee. No board interaction; this touches no protocol bytes and no timing, so bench validation is inapplicable rather than deferred.

Not merging — opened for review.

body:
Wave 3 of per-partner LLM BYOK (#3228, spec §4 in `docs/superpowers/specs/ai-mcp/2026-08-23-per-partner-llm-byok-design.md`). **Track always, deduct never for partner-keyed usage, budgets unchanged.** This closes the deliberate W02 gap where BYOK partners would have double-billed — must merge before any release ships the feature.

Closes #3886

## What's in

- **`billing_source` stamps** on `ai_cost_usage` + `ai_sessions` (migration `2026-09-06`, additive with named CHECKs; both columns classified `included` in `CORE_TENANT_EXPORT_POLICY`). The aggregate stamp is a most-recent-writer label — deduction is decided per-turn, never from the column. Sessions are stamped at create.
- **Entitlement/credits split**: `checkBillingCredits` still enforces the plan gate for everyone (BYOK is not a plan bypass), but the credits-exhausted denial and `deductBillingCredits` run only for `'platform'`-sourced usage.
- **Source threading**: all nine record/check call sites pass the source from the same resolution that produced the key actually used (SDK sites read the immutable session snapshot). `billingSource` is a required parameter — no default, so a future call site can't silently deduct credits for BYOK turns.
- **`GET /ai/usage` reports `billedTo`** via a decrypt-free existence read (`getLlmBillingSourceForOrg`) — a dashboard poll never touches key material, never writes config state, never 500s on a missing org.

## Review

One independent round (code-reviewer + silent-failure-hunter); both confirmed the caller sweep complete and the split correct, and their findings landed in `e7666bf9e` — notably the usage-poll decrypt/write side-effect and a fail-open org lookup in the ticket draft.

## Verification

`tsc` clean; 299 tests across the touched suites green locally. **Integration test on real Postgres**: a partner-keyed turn stamps `billing_source='partner_key'` with zero billing-service calls, and the platform control proves the deduct fires at the right URL — reruns in the blocking `integration-test` job with the export-policy suites.

author: misnow1
body:
Implements the Phase 2 design recorded in `docs/sd-image.md`. Prepare a card at the bench, put it in a Pi, and it provisions itself on first boot — no shell session, no Go toolchain, and **no Internet** once the release tarball is staged.

## The flow

```bash
./deploy/pi/prep-card.sh --site my-venue.yaml --ssh-key ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
```

`prep-card.sh` finds the mounted boot partition, **validates the site config with `combiner -check` before writing anything**, substitutes the public key into the cloud-init template, and stages the release tarballs + `SHA256SUMS`. A bad VLAN id is caught at a desk, not on a dark unit in a rack.

Guards: refuses any volume without `config.txt`/`cmdline.txt`, rejects a private key passed where a public one was meant, and warns if the SSH placeholder survives (that card would come up console-only).

Windows is a documented three-file copy — the boot partition is FAT32, so it is visible in both Finder and Explorer.

## What lands on the card

`deploy/pi/cloud-init/` — `user-data` with an explicit `EDIT THIS BLOCK` section (replacing Imager's user-data also replaces the login it configured, so the account has to be defined there), and `combiner-firstboot.sh`, which verifies and unpacks the tarball, places `site.yaml`, and hands off to **`install.sh`** — still the single tested install path.

Everything is logged to the FAT partition, because diagnosing a headless unit means pulling the card and reading it on a laptop, which cannot mount the ext4 root. A failure prints a `PROVISIONING FAILED` banner and leaves IP forwarding **off**.

## Why not ship a downloadable `.img`

Imager 2.x assumes `init_format: none` for a local `.img` — customisation is declared in a hosted `os_list` manifest, not in the image. A downloadable image today would be a *worse* experience than this. The image is still the goal, but it just bakes in this contract, so the contract comes first.

## Verification

Tested end-to-end in `debian:trixie` **arm64** containers against the real **v0.1.0** release:

| Scenario | Result |
|---|---|
| With network | apt installs the 4 runtime packages; staged binary reports `combiner 0.1.0` |
| `--network none`, packages preinstalled | `all runtime dependencies present — skipping apt` — never touches the network |

Both stop only at `modprobe 8021q`, which no container can satisfy. The offline run is the racked-Pi scenario proven working, and the first run is the first native execution confirming the v0.1.0 version stamp.

**That container run caught a real bug**: `sha256sum -c | grep -q ": OK"` fails under `pipefail` — grep exits on the first match, SIGPIPEs `sha256sum`, and the pipeline reports 141. Now uses `--status` and the exit code, which also fixes the checksum passing whenever some *other* staged file verified.

## Also

- `shellcheck` target wired into `make check` and CI (previously ungated)
- pytest coverage parsing `user-data` and pinning the contracts `prep-card.sh` depends on: the SSH placeholder, the firstboot path, the site filename
- `prep-card.sh` and `cloud-init/` now ship in release packages

## Summary

`main` has been red since the merge batch, for a reason outside our source: `.github/workflows/build.yml` takes its toolchain from `treeform/setup-nim-action@v6` without pinning nimby, that action started shipping nimby `0.2.0`, and `nimby sync nimby.lock -g` under 0.2.0 no longer leaves packages where the compiler's search path looks — so every dependency import fails to resolve:

```
src/ctf.nim(3, 11) Error: cannot open file: bitworld/runtime
src/ctf/sim.nim(8, 10) Error: cannot open file: bitworld/pixelfonts
src/ctf/sim.nim(10, 3)  Error: cannot open file: pixie
```

The evidence that it is the toolchain and not the tree: the same SHA builds clean locally, the failure appears identically on seven consecutive main runs regardless of their contents, and the one CI job that passes (`wasm-replay-viewer`) is the one whose Dockerfile pins nimby explicitly.

Fix is to pin nimby in CI to the version our container builds already prove works (`0.1.26`), in both the native `build` job and the arena job, keeping each job's existing Nim version.

**RFC:** RFC-0019 · **Rama:** `feat/rfc-0019-sondeo-del-corpus` · **Commits:** `1331e96..3e84a2a`

**Bloques sin criterio propio:** la migración (`ce2b9ec`, `e5b0fcf` → `321a811`), la configuración de §8 (`e746314` → `e45292d`) y la CLI de §7 (`c54c6a7` → `3b62201`).

**CA-11, CA-14 y CA-15 no son de este PR:** el DoR (#55, PR #56) los movió a RFC-0010 y RFC-0020, que es donde se construye lo que verifican.

### Forma del ciclo (RFC-0014 §6.1.1)

Decidida antes de empezar, no sobre la marcha:

- **Suite completa** para la migración: bloque DDL atómico, revertirlo enrojece a la vez la forma del esquema y el comportamiento de `ck_watcher_outcome`.
- **Por criterio** para el sondeo, agrupando solo lo que comparte unidad de implementación: las tres salidas tempranas y el latido son ramas del mismo esqueleto de `run_once`; el *lease* es una función; la promoción es otra.

### Cobertura

```
app/ingestion/watcher.py     150 stmts    0 miss    100%
app/ingestion/               (conjunto)             ≥95%
app/core/settings.py          17 stmts    0 miss    100%
TOTAL                        768 stmts   21 miss     97%
```

Umbral del DoD: ≥80 % global, ≥95 % en `app/ingestion/`. Cumplidos.

### Autocomprobación por reversión — encontró dos tests que no probaban nada

La comprobación #3 del prompt (RFC-0014 A-6, TDD-3) es la que importa, y **falló en dos criterios**:

| Criterio | Con la implementación revertida | Causa |
|---|---|---|
| **CA-6** | quedó **VERDE** | Afirmaba `outcome != OUTCOME_INDEXED`. Con el guardia del *lease* invertido, el ciclo intentaba indexar, el `_ExplodingEmbedder` lanzaba `AssertionError`, el manejador de fallos la capturaba y devolvía `failed` — también distinto de `indexed`. |
| **CA-13** | quedó **VERDE** *incluso quitando los dos rollbacks* | Hacía fallar al **embebedor**, y eso no prueba ningún rollback: `index_corpus` embebe TODO antes de escribir NADA, así que el fallo ocurre antes de la primera escritura y no hay nada que revertir. |

Corregidos en `3e84a2a`, **sin tocar ninguna implementación** — los dos tests *pasaban* y se endurecieron, que es lo contrario de P-9. CA-6 exige ahora exactamente `OUTCOME_UNSTABLE` en el informe y en el latido. CA-13 inyecta el fallo en `_upsert_chunk` a mitad de la escritura (mismo patrón que RFC-0002 CA-7) y cambia **más de una unidad**, porque `index_corpus` solo reescribe los fragmentos cuyo `content_hash` difiere y con uno solo la escritura nunca está «a medias». El `assert llamadas["n"] >= 2` impide que vuelva a degradarse en silencio.

Reversión sobre el resto, todos **ROJO**: CA-1, CA-7, CA-12, CA-16, CA-17, CA-18, y CA-3 (documentada en `6e9f4d5`).

### Desviaciones respecto al RFC

1. **`run_once(conn, embedder, settings)` recibe las tres dependencias explícitas.** §3 describe el algoritmo, no la firma. Mismo patrón que `index_corpus` de RFC-0002, que el propio §2 declara como el ingestor que se invoca.
2. **Un ciclo que no puede reclamar el *lease* deja el latido en `unstable`,** con `detail = {"reason": "lease_held"}`. `ck_watcher_outcome` cierra el vocabulario y ninguno de los valores dice «ocupado»; `unstable` es el único que significa lo mismo —ciclo perdido a propósito, el siguiente lo recoge— y **no marca `last_success_at`**, que sería lo grave.
3. **Los reintentos reutilizan la detección pendiente del mismo contenido** en vez de generar un ULID nuevo cada ciclo. Sin esto `attempt_count` nunca acumula, nunca llega al tope y el sondeo reintenta para siempre: **CA-12 sería inimplementable**. El RFC no lo especifica; §3 paso 6 lo insinúa al decir que el `UNIQUE` sobre `idempotency_key` *«absorbe una ejecución que muriera tras el paso 5»*.
4. **El corte del *dead letter* tiene dos puertas, no una.** `_is_dead_lettered` impide que el ciclo siguiente vuelva a detectar el mismo contenido agotado y abra otro trabajo. Sin esa segunda puerta el bucle infinito entra por la detección en vez de por el reintento — y el RFC solo cerraba la primera. Recogido en el texto de CA-12 por PR #62.
5. **La CLI mapea el resultado a código de salida** (`missing_corpus` → 2, `failed` y `dead_lettered` → 1, el resto → 0). El `cron` no lee el latido: lee el código de salida y lo escribe en la bitácora, y es lo único que un operador ve sin abrir la base.
6. **CA-3 se declara heredado de RFC-0002 CA-5** (RFC-0014 §6.1.2). La invariante —contenido idéntico no regenera embeddings— la entrega el *diffing* por `content_hash` de `index_corpus`, no código de este RFC. Romperlo a propósito para volver a arreglarlo sería peor que la brecha. **Reversión verificada y documentada en `6e9f4d5`:** con `force=True` el test falla con `AssertionError: el camino de contenido identico no puede embeber`.
7. **`test_migrations_head` fija el *head* del árbol como literal**, y toda migración lo rompe. No se actualizó junto a la migración —eso sería P-9— sino al revés: afirmar que el *head* es la revisión de este RFC **es** afirmar que la migración existe y está bien encadenada, así que esa afirmación entró en rojo antes de que el fichero existiera (`e5b0fcf`, `b2272cf`).

body: ## Summary - **Universe archive**: Register ~1500–2500 US index tickers (S&P 500/400/600, Nasdaq-100, Russell 2000) via Wikipedia lists; tagged `univ:*` so they stay out of the trading desk sidebar by default. - **Bulk download workflow**: One-time full history archive + daily incremental refresh with overlap days (CLI `scripts/bulk_archive.py` and Data tab SSE buttons). - **Setup scanner**: Scan stored OHLCV for EP, near-high, volume surge, breakout queue, Darvas box/breakout/fail, RSI OB/OS — with filter pills and Chart / + Desk actions. - **Desk workflow**: Sidebar "Desk only" filter; promote universe symbols to desk; metrics scanner and setup scan default to full universe when data exists. ## Workflow ```bash python3 scripts/bulk_archive.py --sync-indices all python3 scripts/bulk_archive.py --archive --start 2000-01-01 --delay 1.5 python3 scripts/bulk_archive.py --refresh --overlap-days 5 --delay 0.8 ``` Or: **Data** tab → Sync indices → Archive history → Daily refresh. Then: **Scanner** → Setup scan; promote names to desk; charts / Adaptive Trend / KNN / Statistics on any symbol with stored bars. ## Tests `DATA_SERVICE_MODE=embedded python3 -m unittest discover tests` — **55/55** passing.
